content:
Apple has been ordered to respond by Monday to a complaint filed by Epic Games with Brazil's antitrust regulator. Epic accuses Apple of interpreting its obligations under a recent App Store antitrust agreement in Brazil in a restrictive manner. Details below.

A little background

Two months ago, Apple announced it would allow developers in Brazil to distribute their apps through alternative app marketplaces.

The change was part of a settlement that ended a multi-year antitrust investigation. The investigation stemmed from a complaint filed by Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre over Apple's App Store rules.

Under the new terms, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps through alternative app marketplaces and use payment options outside of Apple's IAP system.

Apple also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% "Core Technology Fee" on sales of digital goods and services for apps distributed through channels outside the App Store. More details on the structure here.

Epic questions Apple's implementation

According to a report today in Brazilian newspaper O Globo (relayed by MacMagazine), Epic recently filed a petition with Brazilian antitrust regulator CADE, accusing Apple of setting up "structural, technical, and access barriers" that undermine the practical viability of alternative app distribution.

Epic pointed out that, although the new Brazilian terms apply only to iOS apps, Apple's agreement with CADE "expressly covers iPadOS."

Epic is also reportedly challenging so-called "scare sheets" — prompts designed to discourage users from installing apps from outside the App Store. Epic also challenged the current installation process, claiming it requires nine steps, compared to six used by Apple in Europe.

O Globo reports that Epic further pointed out that Apple's original installation process in Europe required 15 steps, but after being asked to cut it to six, "the download abandonment rate fell from 65% to 25%."

Finally, Epic told CADE that Apple's reporting requirements "go far beyond what is necessary to calculate fees," allowing the company "to monitor competitors' business models."

O Globo says CADE has given Apple until Monday to respond. Apple has not publicly commented on the matter.
